question_text: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of pain during intercourse and vaginal dryness. The patient has also had intermittent hot flashes and fatigue during this time. Over the past year, her periods have become irregular. Her last menstrual period was over six months ago. She is sexually active with one partner and does not use protection or contraception. She has a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia during childhood, which has remained in remission. Pelvic examination shows an atrophic cervix and vagina. A urinary pregnancy test is negative. A progestin challenge test is performed and shows no withdrawal bleeding. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Question
                    A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of pain during intercourse and vaginal dryness. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

The 23-year-old woman presents with symptoms indicative of ovarian insufficiency, including irregular periods, vaginal dryness, and no withdrawal bleeding on progestin challenge. These findings suggest low estrogen levels, which typically lead to increased FSH levels due to lack of negative feedback from estrogen on the pituitary gland. The progestin challenge test showing no withdrawal bleeding further supports anovulation. Given her history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which can impact ovarian function, it is likely that her ovarian reserve is diminished. Therefore, the most consistent finding in this case would be an increased FSH to LH ratio, as FSH levels rise in response to low estrogen production. The evidence path regarding anovulation and its association with hormonal imbalance supports this conclusion. Thus, the best-supported answer is an increased FSH to LH ratio.
